models.section: 4.1 Sub-model I: Cost-benefit Analysis Considering Marginal Effects
models.purpose: Represent municipal and resident tourism income, diminishing per-tourist spending, and increasing infrastructure cost as a function of tourist volume and tax.
models.summary: The branch starts from net municipal economic benefit, decomposes tourist consumption between government and residents, attenuates per-tourist spending through two logistic-like factors, and subtracts fixed plus quadratic infrastructure cost.

Consumption threshold set to 1.5 times A0.
Tourist spending allocated to residents in tourism industries.
Coefficient multiplying squared tourist volume in government cost.
Fixed public-service expenditure.

governing_equations.purpose: Define the economic objective as municipal revenue minus municipal cost.
Define total tourist consumption from adjusted consumption per tourist and tourist count.

governing_equations.source_expression: alpha = A0 / [(1 + exp(k0 A0 Nt (t-tbasic)))(1 + exp(k0(A0-A0max)))]
governing_equations.purpose: Attenuate per-tourist consumption with volume/tax and consumption-threshold factors.
Decompose tourist consumption into municipal and resident revenue.

governing_equations.source_expression: C_Gi = alpha Nt t; C_Ri = alpha Nt (1-t)
governing_equations.purpose: Allocate tourist consumption between government and residents by tax share.
Model government cost as quadratic tourist-volume cost plus fixed expenditure.

equation_status.reason: Equations (1)-(6) were visually checked on pages 7-9.

objectives: Maximize E over admissible tourist volume and policy settings.
constraints: E must be positive in the coupled feasible set.
Tourist count is bounded by the coupled model's Ntmax constraint.
Tax and consumption conventions must be consistent with parameter units.

details: Static algebraic model has no time initial state.
The paper later requires 0 < Nt < Ntmax and E > 0.
Policy response is assumed instantaneous, so outputs are interpreted as a static partial equilibrium.

parameter_estimation.method: A0 and tax are attributed broadly to government sources; k0, Ci, and related coefficients are labeled estimates without a fitting protocol.

steps: Evaluate adjusted alpha for candidate Nt and t.
Compute total consumption and government/resident shares.
Compute quadratic plus fixed government cost.
Return E and related revenue outputs to the coupled objective.
software: Python is disclosed in the AI-use report, but no executable script is supplied.
algorithm.convergence_criteria: Not applicable to the algebraic branch; the outer SLSQP criteria are omitted.

assumptions: Per-tourist spending begins from a constant basic value.
Diminishing benefit is encoded through the chosen attenuation expression.
Government cost grows quadratically with tourist volume.
The tax share partitions all modeled tourist consumption between government and residents.

identifiability_feasibility.analysis: Several coefficients are labeled estimates, no independent anchors or uncertainty ranges are given, and the unit requirements of the exponential arguments are not stated.

validation_refs: Figure 4 schematic economic response on page 9.
Figure 8 economic constraint heatmap on page 16.
Figure 9 Juneau economic response on page 17.
models.computational_cost: Constant work per candidate policy setting; the paper does not report outer-grid or solver evaluation counts.
strengths: Separates municipal revenue, resident revenue, and government cost.
Makes diminishing benefit and increasing cost visible before optimization.
limitations: The attenuation expression is uncalibrated and dimensionally unclear.
Quadratic cost and spending allocation are assumed rather than fitted.
Tax units alternate between percent and proportion.
missing_details: Exact data sources and units for every coefficient.
Calibration loss, ranges, and uncertainty.
Executed code and runtime overrides.
Treatment of tourism spending that leaves the local economy.

models.section: 4.2 Sub-model II: Social Welfare Optimization Model
models.purpose: Combine resident income pressure and crowding pressure into a satisfaction proxy and convert it to a monetary social objective.
models.summary: The branch maximizes a monetized satisfaction product. Living pressure is resident tourism income divided by incremental living cost, crowding pressure is residents divided by tourists, their product is the satisfaction indicator, and a logistic-like conversion factor creates Cadd.

variables.definition: Monetized social benefit objective.
Product of living and crowding pressure indicators.

Resident tourism income divided by incremental living cost.
Resident count divided by tourist count, despite being named pressure.

Incremental cost of living attributed to tourism, treated as constant in the prose.
Juneau resident population.
Tourist count and decision variable.
Scale for hidden social benefit, tabulated as 5.
Threshold coefficient applied to resident count in Eq. 10.
Tax rate also used inside the Eq. 10 exponent.

governing_equations.purpose: Define monetized social benefit as satisfaction times its virtual value equivalent.
Define the living and crowding components of satisfaction.
Combine living and crowding components multiplicatively.
Attenuate the satisfaction value equivalent as tourist count relative to residents and tax rises.

equation_status.reason: Equations (7)-(10) were visually checked on pages 10-11.

objectives: Maximize S subject to the coupled social acceptability threshold.
constraints: The coupled model requires S > Smin.
The prose sets the acceptable social range using 60 percent of a 2023 baseline.
Cadd is positive under the displayed logistic form.

details: Static algebraic model has no time initial state.
Nt must be positive and later bounded by Ntmax; S must exceed Smin.
The instantaneous-response assumption supplies a static equilibrium interpretation.

parameter_estimation.method: A1 is described as estimated from an article and k1 as an estimate; no survey, loss function, or fitted uncertainty is shown.

steps: Receive resident revenue from the economic branch.
Compute living and crowding components.
Multiply them to form s.
Compute Cadd and S.
Pass S to the coupled objective and threshold.
algorithm.convergence_criteria: Not applicable to branch equations; outer solver criteria are omitted.

assumptions: Income and congestion jointly determine resident satisfaction.
Incremental resident living cost can be treated as constant.
A product of two ratios is an adequate satisfaction proxy.
Social satisfaction can be monetized with a virtual value equivalent.

identifiability_feasibility.analysis: No resident survey identifies s, A1, k1, or the 60-percent threshold mapping, and the exponent mixes tourist count and tax without declared scale units.

validation_refs: Figure 5 schematic social response on page 11.
Figure 8 social constraint heatmap on page 16.
models.computational_cost: Constant work per candidate policy setting; no calibration or uncertainty computation is reported.
strengths: Keeps resident income and congestion visible as separate components.
Makes the social acceptability threshold explicit in the coupled model.
limitations: The satisfaction proxy has no survey validation.
The meaning and monotonic direction of the pressure ratios are unclear.
missing_details: Resident satisfaction data and measurement model.
Units and provenance for CRc, A1, and k1.
Derivation of the 60-percent constraint.
Sensitivity to alternate aggregations of Pl and Pf.

models.section: 4.3 Sub-model III: Environmental Carrying Capacity Model
models.purpose: Represent attraction-level visitor emissions, a contextual glacier-response relation, tax-funded environmental governance, and monetized carbon loss.
models.summary: The environmental branch minimizes carbon cost minus governance expenditure. It records a glacier recession relation for context, squares allocated visitor counts to produce attraction emissions, sums them, and monetizes total emissions while saturating the governance term.

governing_equations.purpose: Relate carbon-emission change to a contextual glacier volume response; the paper states it is not used in the objective.
Assign a quadratic carbon-emission term to each attraction from allocated tourist count.

governing_equations.source_expression: C_env = N_t A2 t/(1+exp(k2 t)); C_CO2 = C_perC E_CO2
governing_equations.purpose: Compute saturating tax-funded governance and monetized carbon cost.

equation_status.reason: Equations (11)-(15) were visually checked on pages 12-13; Eq. 12 is retained even though the paper excludes it from optimization.

objectives: Minimize Env within the coupled optimization.
Use carbon emissions rather than the contextual glacier equation as the optimized environmental proxy.
constraints: Attraction shares are presented as 0.2, 0.2, and 0.6.
Tourist count and tax share the coupled feasible domain.

details: No dynamic glacier or environmental state is numerically integrated.
Attraction shares are proportions and should sum to one; Nt is positive and bounded in the coupled model.
Environmental governance and visitor allocation are evaluated statically.

parameter_estimation.method: Gamma is attributed to a statistic, r values to contextual tourism statistics, A2 to government, and k2 to estimate; no emissions inventory or fit is shown.

steps: Allocate Nt across attractions using ri.
Compute squared attraction emission terms and sum them.
Compute governance expenditure and carbon cost.
Return Env to the coupled objective.
Optionally display Eq. 12 as contextual glacier response without feeding it into the optimizer.
software: No executable environmental implementation is supplied.
algorithm.convergence_criteria: Not applicable to algebraic branch; outer SLSQP criteria are omitted.

assumptions: Tourist-attraction allocation is represented by fixed shares.
Attraction carbon impact grows with squared allocated tourist count.
A single virtual carbon price converts emissions to economic loss.
Tax-funded governance has diminishing returns.
Eq. 12 is contextual rather than result-bearing in the optimizer.

identifiability_feasibility.analysis: The quadratic emissions law, glacier relation, carbon price, and governance coefficients are not identified from a coherent emissions, climate, or expenditure dataset.

validation_refs: Figure 6 schematic environmental response on page 13.
Figure 8 environmental constraint heatmap on page 16.
Figures 9-10 environmental response curves on page 17.
models.computational_cost: Linear in the number of attraction categories per candidate policy setting; the paper uses three categories and reports no runtime.
strengths: Keeps attraction allocation explicit before aggregating emissions.
Clearly states that the glacier equation is not part of the objective.
Separates governance spending from carbon cost.
limitations: The emissions equation is dimensionally inconsistent with gamma stated per tourist.
The glacier relation combines quantities with incompatible stated meanings and has no local calibration.
Carbon monetization and environmental threshold are unsupported.
missing_details: Attraction-specific emissions inventory.
Units for V0, Delta V, C0, and Delta ECO2.
Source and uncertainty for CperC and k2.
Evidence linking environmental spending to modeled outcomes.

models.section: 4.4 Pareto Optimal Solution for Total Benefit
models.purpose: Combine economic, social, and environmental branch outputs into one weighted objective and impose feasibility constraints over tourist volume.
models.summary: The paper scalarizes three branch outputs with fixed rank-derived weights, enforces sign, social baseline, and visitor-capacity constraints, and sends the resulting problem to SLSQP.

objectives: Maximize the fixed weighted scalar T.
Keep each branch inside its declared feasible domain.

details: Eq. 17 supplies objective and visitor-count bounds.
The static partial-equilibrium assumption is inherited from section 2.

parameter_estimation.method: Weights are normalized from Alaska GDP, cost-of-living, and EPI rank fractions rather than elicited stakeholder tradeoffs; Smin and Ntmax use 2023 baselines.

steps: Evaluate all three branch outputs for a candidate policy setting.
Apply fixed weights and form T.
Reject candidates violating Eq. 17.
Use SLSQP to search the decision space.
Report selected visitor count and objective outputs.
software: SLSQP is named; the implementation package, version, and code are omitted.
algorithm.convergence_criteria: No tolerances, initialization, derivative settings, iteration limit, restart rule, or optimality residual are reported.

assumptions: Economic, social, and environmental outputs can be combined after monetization.
State-level rank fractions represent Juneau objective priorities.
One fixed weight vector is sufficient for the decision.
The 2023 tourist volume is a meaningful capacity bound.
SLSQP's returned point is treated as the selected solution.

identifiability_feasibility.analysis: The paper provides an explicit constraint system and one weight vector, but the normative weights, threshold meanings, inconsistent search/capacity domains, and solver feasibility evidence are not established.

validation_refs: Figure 7 pairwise tradeoff schematics on page 15.
Figures 9-10 objective and rate curves on page 17.
models.computational_cost: Unknown; the paper mentions traversing 0-10 million and SLSQP but supplies neither grid resolution nor evaluation counts.
strengths: Collects branch objectives and all feasibility constraints in adjacent equations.
Keeps the weight derivation visible rather than hiding coefficients.
limitations: One weighted-sum solution is not a Pareto frontier.
SLSQP does not establish global optimality.
Weights are not stakeholder preferences and output scales remain unclear.
The 0-10 million search claim conflicts with Ntmax=1.67 million.
missing_details: Decision-vector definition beyond Nt and policy parameters.
SLSQP configuration and convergence diagnostics.
Pareto set or weight sweep.
Consistent units and normalization for branch objectives.
Feasible-point and constraint-residual table.

models.section: 4.4.2-7 Solver, transfer, policy levers, and sensitivity
models.family: SLSQP scenario transfer and local sensitivity workflow
models.purpose: Apply the coupled model to Juneau and Jiuzhaigou, adjust selected weights and tax parameters, interpret policy levers, and run local one-factor response sweeps.
models.summary: The workflow uses the coupled equations without adding a new numbered formula. Juneau and Jiuzhaigou receive different weights and selected parameters, SLSQP or traversal yields headline visitor counts, and dispersion, tax, and consumption are perturbed one factor at a time.

variables.definition: Reported visitor decision for each destination.
Coupled objective output.
Policy lever and transferred parameter.
Tourist-dispersion lever represented by attraction share.
Tourist consumption policy/input lever.
Destination-specific economic, social, environmental weights.
Juneau or Jiuzhaigou scenario.

equation_status.reason: This workflow reuses Eqs. (1)-(18); no additional transfer, SLSQP, sensitivity, or expenditure-feedback equation is printed.

objectives: Find a destination-specific visitor count under the coupled scalar objective.
Describe the direction of response to local changes in r, t, and A0.
Translate model controls into tourism management measures.
constraints: The coupled Eq. 17 constraints are inherited.
Juneau and Jiuzhaigou parameter adjustments should be source-supported.
Local sensitivity changes one stated factor at a time in the reported plots.

details: No SLSQP starting point or restart policy is reported.
Figures and prose use conflicting tourist-count, tax, and consumption ranges.
Each city is treated as a static equilibrium under its chosen parameters.

parameter_estimation.method: Jiuzhaigou tax is set to 13 percent and weights to 0.625, 0.313, 0.062; other key parameters are described as approximately Juneau's. Sensitivity perturbs r, t, and A0 around selected values.

steps: Choose destination context and parameter vector.
Evaluate the coupled model across candidate visitor volumes and/or call SLSQP.
Select the reported optimum.
Perturb r, t, and A0 locally and regenerate visitor/objective curves.
Compare response shapes across cities.
Translate directions into memo recommendations.
software: SLSQP and Python are mentioned, but no code, package version, or configuration is provided.
algorithm.convergence_criteria: Omitted: no optimality tolerance, feasibility tolerance, iteration budget, restart rule, or comparison against alternative starts.

assumptions: The same functional forms transfer between destinations.
Selected parameter changes capture relevant city differences.
Local one-factor response curves are adequate for policy discussion.
Similar curve shapes indicate transferable structure.

identifiability_feasibility.analysis: Jiuzhaigou parameters are not fitted to a reproducible destination dataset, SLSQP evidence is absent, and local one-factor curves do not establish global sensitivity or model transfer validity.

validation_refs: Figures 9-10 destination response panels on page 17.
Figures 11-12 key-parameter response curves on pages 18-19.
Figures 13-14 local sensitivity plots on pages 20-21.
models.computational_cost: Unknown; no number of candidate points, SLSQP evaluations, perturbation grid size, or runtime is stated.
strengths: Separates an invariant model structure from destination-specific parameter adjustments in the prose.
Keeps three policy levers visible across result, sensitivity, table, and memo sections.
Uses aligned plots to compare two cases.
limitations: No reproducible transfer calibration or external validation.
Local one-factor sweeps cannot rank importance under interactions.
The expenditure plan is not fed back into model parameters or re-optimization.
Memo numbers drift from model meanings and units.
missing_details: Destination datasets and exact parameter-source mapping.
Executed solver configuration and outputs.
Sensitivity ranges, fixed factors, and numerical tables.
Feedback equations from spending to capacity, satisfaction, demand, or environment.
Independent validation outcomes for either city.

dependency_edges.handoff: Economic objective E and revenue components enter the scalar objective and policy interpretation.
Social objective S enters the scalar objective and social feasibility constraint.
Environmental balance Env enters the scalar objective and environmental feasibility constraint.
The coupled equations, constraints, and weight structure are reused for both destinations, local sensitivity, and memo recommendations.
